full_story_part1.text: There was a small twist. A service let people ask AI to make phone calls. But humans were making some calls behind the scenes. This was part of a test. The main service was Muse, Meta's AI assistant. Muse can call businesses and stores in the United States. It can book haircuts, check if items are in stock, and ask for price estimates. If AI can handle difficult phone calls, it seems very useful. But in some tests of its calling feature, trained human contract workers made the calls instead of AI. They spoke with people until each conversation ended.

full_story_part1.canonical_text:
There was a small twist. A service let people ask AI to make phone calls. But humans were making some calls behind the scenes. This was part of a test.

The main service was Muse, Meta’s AI assistant. Muse can call businesses and stores in the United States. It can book haircuts, check if items are in stock, and ask for price estimates. If AI can handle difficult phone calls, it seems very useful.

But in some tests of its calling feature, trained human contract workers made the calls instead of AI. They spoke with people until each conversation ended.

full_story_part2.text: The problem was not that humans made the calls. The problem was how users were told who was speaking. People who asked Muse to make a call might think AI was doing it. But sometimes, a human was speaking instead. If this was not explained clearly, users could not know if it was AI or a person. They enjoyed the ease of AI. But they did not know that a human was on the other end. This was happening behind the scenes. Also, a call might need user information to continue. That information might then be shared by mistake with contract workers at a call center. Meta employees raised this inside the company as a privacy concern.

People who asked Muse to make a call might think AI was doing it. But sometimes, a human was speaking instead. If this was not explained clearly, users could not know if it was AI or a person. They enjoyed the ease of AI. But they did not know that a human was on the other end. This was happening behind the scenes.

Also, a call might need user information to continue. That information might then be shared by mistake with contract workers at a call center. Meta employees raised this inside the company as a privacy concern.

full_story_part3.text: News reports also quoted a report from an employee. It said that human staff made inappropriate comments about race during calls to bargain over internet or cable fees. However, this is only one report. It would be wrong to say this about all contract workers. A Meta executive admitted that starting the test without explaining it clearly was a mistake. The company also changed the human concierge feature back to how it was before, at least for now. The real challenge for AI phone calls is not only how they speak. It is also whether they can honestly tell people who is on the other end. The more useful a service is, the less it should hide the people working behind the scenes. The Muse case showed this simple but important point.
